episodes.title: Dr. Ramani Says “Narcissism” Isn’t a Diagnosis. I Agree.
episodes.description:
Dr. Mark Ettensohn examines a recent interview between Dr. Ramani Durvasula and filmmaker Mark Vicente, focusing on Dr. Ramani’s statement that “narcissism” is not a diagnosis.

Dr. Ettensohn agrees with this clarification. Narcissism is not itself a DSM diagnosis, and the term is used in many different ways across clinical psychology, personality research, psychodynamic theory, and popular culture. The episode explores what follows from that observation and asks whether public discussions of narcissism remain grounded in coherent psychological models.

The discussion examines how broad terms such as “narcissism” can gradually shift in meaning while continuing to support increasingly specific claims about personality, motivation, empathy, treatment resistance, manipulation, and interpersonal behavior. Dr. Ettensohn argues that ambiguous or loosely defined psychological constructs should not be used to explain complex human behavior.

The episode also considers what is omitted from many popular discussions of narcissism, including identity disturbance, depression, anxiety, suicidality, developmental trauma, assessment, and treatment. Dr. Ettensohn argues that reducing narcissism primarily to a collection of abusive or manipulative qualities risks separating the construct from established models of psychopathology while retaining the trappings of clinical authority.

The episode concludes by discussing why conceptual precision matters in psychology and why public education about personality pathology should strive to reflect coherent psychological theory rather than popular stereotypes.

episodes.title: Decoding NPD: The Critical Role of Attachment
episodes.description:
In this video, Dr. Ettensohn draws heavily on his own research concerning pathological narcissism and attachment patterns, using attachment theory as a lens to focus explanatory power onto the often confusing dynamics of NPD. 

Beginning with a general overview of Bartholomew's four-prototype model of adult attachment, Dr. Ettensohn identifies the most common attachment patterns of individuals with NPD. He describes the relevant research on the development of these patterns and draws parallels with descriptions of early care deficits thought to cause pathological narcissism.
